By incorporating a bias towards low-reward actions, the approach aims to promote diversity in an agent's behavior. In contrast, the approach has been found to have a negative impact on performance when rewards are present. Experimental results demonstrate that this modified approach can improve an agent's performance in environments where rewards are present, without compromising its ability to learn from rewards. Additionally, the approach has been found to have a positive impact on performance when rewards are absent. The field of reinforcement learning (RL) has made significant advancements in recent years, largely due to the creation of the OpenAI Gym. However, the Gym's current capabilities are insufficient to tackle the complex challenges in real-world RL applications. To address this, there is an urgent need for a more comprehensive and realistic benchmark that incorporates multiple features from real-world RL scenarios. To fill this gap, we have developed the URLB: Unsupervised Reward Learning Benchmark. This innovative benchmark is designed to simulate real-world RL tasks by incorporating diverse features such as multi-episode rewards, sparse rewards, continuous control, and self-supervised learning tasks. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we have evaluated various state-of-the-art RL algorithms on URLB and found that none of them were able to achieve satisfactory performance across all tasks. This highlights the need for further research to develop more robust RL algorithms that can handle the diverse challenges in real-world RL scenarios. By releasing URLB, we aim to accelerate the development of more practical RL algorithms and improve the understanding of their strengths and weaknesses in real-world RL settings. This study introduces a dataset for evaluating image matching in low-light conditions.  The dataset consists of 60,000 pairs of images with significant illumination differences.  A novel method is proposed to create the dataset, involving the collection of real-world pairs of low-light and well-lit images and the generation of synthetic pairs through image processing.  A comprehensive evaluation is conducted using the newly created dataset, with the performance of state-of-the-art image matching algorithms being assessed and compared.  The results indicate that current algorithms struggle to generalize to matching tasks in low-light conditions.  The dataset is publicly available at https://github.com/zhongyuew/LOWLIGHT-MATCHING. Further details about the study can be found in the accompanying technical report.

GANs have become a popular solution for data generation, but training them is often complicated by a common problem known as mode collapse. This study's results are supported by Hessian eigenvalues and are consistent with previous research on mode collapse. This comprehensive study is the first to use Hessian analysis to understand mode collapse in GANs, providing a new perspective on the phenomenon. Our work also aims to guide future research on mode collapse by identifying areas that require further investigation. The process of removing haze from images is known to introduce distortions and affect the overall visual quality. To address this issue, a new method for evaluating the quality of dehazed images has been developed, focusing on the relationship between haze removal and visual perception. This approach, called Partial Discrepancy to Blind Perception (PDBP), is based on the understanding that haze reduces visual information and dehazing aims to restore lost details. To measure the quality of dehazed images, PDBP compares the visual information recovered through dehazing with the complete visual experience, using a metric that reflects the disparity between restored and original images. This metric, called the Complete Visual Discrepancy (CVD), is designed to capture the full visual experience, and PDBP-based metrics are shown to outperform existing full-reference metrics in evaluating the quality of dehazed images, offering a more comprehensive understanding of the dehazing process. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the PDBP framework in improving dehazed image quality assessment. The accompanying code and datasets are available at https://github.com/zhkang/PDBF-DH-QA. This research has been accepted for publication in the IEEE Transactions on Image Processing. Deep learning models have become the backbone of numerous critical systems, 
but they are vulnerable to a subtle form of attack known as the Deep Learning 
black-box backdoor assault. This type of attack allows an attacker to secretly 
alter a model's behavior by manipulating it, and then trigger a desired outcome 
by feeding in specific data. Existing methods for this type of attack are often 
limited by the need for prior knowledge of model architecture or access to model 
training data, making them impractical in real-world settings. 

In this research, we introduce a new, practical method for backdoor attacks that 
requires no prior knowledge of model architecture or access to model training data. 
The attack works by injecting a malicious payload into the model's parameters, 
which is then activated to alter the model's output. We tested our method on a range 
of models and datasets and found it to be highly effective, with an average success 
rate of 95% across different deep learning models. This research provides a new 
approach to backdoor attacks and highlights the need for improved security 
mechanisms in deep learning models. The accompanying code for this research can 
be found on GitHub at https://github.com/zhkxungo/DeepPayload. A video

This research presents a novel hierarchical control approach for quadruped robots to achieve stable locomotion and secure manipulation in diverse environments. The proposed system integrates two control mechanisms: a lower-level adaptive controller that ensures reliable and robust locomotion, and an upper-level nonlinear controller that optimizes gait planning and coordination for manipulation tasks. The adaptive lower-level controller utilizes Lyapunov design and sliding mode control to address nonlinearities and external disturbances, while the upper-level nonlinear controller uses input-output linearization and feedback linearization to regulate the end-effector's position and orientation. The two controllers are interconnected via a feedback loop to synchronize the end-effector's reference trajectory with the robot's joint velocities. The hierarchical control approach is validated through simulations and experiments on the Cubot robot, demonstrating its effectiveness in various contact-rich environments. The proposed system successfully enables the robot to achieve stable walking and secure manipulation, even in the presence of model uncertainties and external disturbances. The hierarchical control approach is versatile and can be easily adapted for use with diverse robots. The accompanying video demonstrates the system's performance in several challenging scenarios. This technique is shown to significantly improve the translation quality and reduce compilation time.  This paper also explores the potential of the proposed tree-to-tree translation model for use in other programming languages, and the results suggest that it can be successfully applied to the translation of several other languages, including OpenCL kernels, which are commonly used in modern computing systems. This paper also discusses the potential limitations of the proposed tree-to-tree translation model, and the future directions for its application in the translation of programming languages. We introduce a novel, distributed learning approach for classifying melanoma images, leveraging the Personal Wellness Train framework. This framework empowers multiple, independent agents to collectively classify melanoma images, thanks to a shared, common neural network. Each agent is assigned a unique set of images, and periodically exchanges information with neighboring agents. Through this cooperation, the agents' shared neural network evolves, enabling the collective classification of new images. This distributed learning strategy was tested on the ISIC 2018 dataset and yielded competitive results compared to other methods. Notably, the approach enables real-time classification of images, and the shared neural network allows for transfer learning, paving the way for further applications. The associated code is publicly available on GitHub. Our method has the potential to significantly reduce the computational resources required for training machine learning models, particularly in fields like medical image analysis. This shared neural network approach can also facilitate collaborative learning among healthcare professionals, and the common neural network can serve as a knowledge repository. Furthermore, the Personal Wellness Train framework offers a flexible platform for exploring new applications of distributed learning in medical image analysis. To address this limitation, we developed a machine learning-based examination that can be universally applied. Using a dataset from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, we trained a logistic regression model to predict the presence of Alzheimer's disease based on various speech feature sets. The results showed that a combination of acoustic and linguistic features achieved the highest accuracy in predicting the disease, outperforming models relying solely on acoustic or linguistic features. Furthermore, our findings suggest that certain speech features, such as the first-order derivatives of pitch and formants, play a critical role in predicting Alzheimer's, while the significance of other features, including prosodic and linguistic features, remains uncertain. To facilitate further research, we have made our code publicly available on GitHub. Our goal is to provide a foundation for the development of universally applicable examinations for predicting Alzheimer's disease. Few-shot learning, a task that involves adapting to new classes with limited data, is typically achieved by adjusting a pre-trained model to suit the new data distribution. This process, however, is often hindered by the lack of available meta-data, which makes it difficult to accurately assess the model's performance. This limitation is particularly problematic in scenarios where the test data distribution significantly diverges from the training data distribution. Our proposed solution, a meta-filter, offers a practical approach to this challenge by leveraging a combination of meta-data, class labels, and test data to estimate the pre-activation feature space's likelihood. This enables the model to dynamically adjust its predictions based on the likelihood of the test data, thus providing a more accurate assessment of its performance. Our experiments demonstrate that this method effectively addresses the issue of few-shot learning, particularly under conditions of extreme data distribution shift. This breakthrough has significant implications, enabling the accurate detection of sounds without the need for prior labeling, and is expected to be highly adaptable across various datasets. Moreover, we've identified several avenues for future investigation, including the development of a three-dimensional sound detection method. Ultimately, we've successfully demonstrated that our approach can be a valuable addition to the machine learning community. In recent years, deep learning has become increasingly dependent on large amounts of data, but protecting sensitive information poses a significant challenge. This approach involves training a data transformation network using an autoencoder that can restore original data, then applying a random noise layer to the encoded input. The transformed features are then mapped back to the original representation, effectively preserving privacy and utility. This method is particularly effective in handling complex data, including images and videos, which other anonymization techniques struggle to protect. A major threat to facial recognition systems, known as backdoor attacks, arises from maliciously introduced backdoors that can compromise the security and privacy of sensitive information stored in facial recognition models. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in mitigating various backdoor attacks with remarkable accuracy. This paper also showcases the practical application of the proposed method in real-world scenarios, highlighting its potential as a robust defense mechanism against backdoor attacks. The proposed positioning algorithm is also demonstrated to be effective in real-world contextual bandit applications, such as the OpenBand dataset. The task of identifying dead pixels on an display is a complex one, requiring the comparison of an image with a reference image to pinpoint the faulty pixels. However, the process of aligning these two images at a subpixel level is a significant challenge, especially when utilizing deep learning algorithms. To address this issue, we introduce a novel approach that utilizes the Effective Receptive Field to calculate the position of each pixel, thereby facilitating the comparison process without the need for subpixel alignment. Our proposed method is straightforward to implement and can be integrated into existing CNN-based dead pixel detection models with minimal modifications, as demonstrated by its successful application to the DPD dataset. Our experiments show that this method can achieve comparable or even superior results in terms of both accuracy and efficiency, while also providing a more accurate assessment of pixel location. Additionally, we release our code and models for public use at https://github.com/ChenChengYu/DPD. Our approach is expected to have a significant impact on the dead pixel detection task and potentially other applications requiring precise pixel positioning. Deep Neural Networks have become essential components in various computer vision applications, but their widespread adoption is hindered by the high energy consumption of inference processing. To overcome this challenge, we propose a novel edge/cloud collaborative framework called AppealNet, which optimizes DNN inference for embedded systems. AppealNet's architecture is tailored to take advantage of the unique capabilities of edge and cloud systems, allowing it to leverage their combined processing power while minimizing energy consumption. To address the resulting computational demands, AppealNet employs a hierarchical decision-making approach that allows for the efficient use of both systems' resources. We demonstrate AppealNet's effectiveness through its application in a mobile application, which significantly reduces energy consumption by 95% compared to traditional approaches while maintaining high image quality. AppealNet also outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of both energy efficiency and image quality. Comprehensive simulations conducted on a range of platforms further confirm AppealNet's exceptional performance capabilities. AppealNet's highly scalable design also enables it to adapt to a wide range of applications, from resource-constrained embedded systems to high-performance data centers. As a result, AppealNet offers a highly promising solution for the rapidly growing field of computer vision applications. The proposed FlexMatch approach has been extensively tested on image classification tasks and has demonstrated superior results compared to current state-of-the-art methods on standard datasets. Furthermore, CPL can be seamlessly applied to other semi-supervised learning methods to further enhance their performance. Predicting and preventing traffic accidents can be achieved through early
anticipation of such incidents. This study proposes a novel method called Dynamic
Spatial-Temporal Focus Network (DSTFocus), which leverages a dynamic attention
mechanism to identify potential safety risks in traffic video footage. The proposed
approach models risk factors as a dynamic set of focus points and updates this set
dynamically based on past history and future predictions. The DSTFocus network employs
a dual-attention mechanism to dynamically focus on safety risks and aggregate
relevant features from various points. The proposed method outperforms existing
approaches in terms of accuracy and state-of-the-art performance on two public datasets.

Our research introduces Entailer, a question-answering system that generates a step-by-step logical reasoning process to support its answers, aiming for accuracy and truthfulness. Unlike existing methods that solely focus on generating answers, Entailer's primary goal is to provide a transparent and supported response. To achieve this, we developed a pipeline that first identifies possible supporting facts and then constructs a logical reasoning chain to link these facts and answer, ensuring a step-by-step progression from given premises to the answer, without jumping to the final answer directly. Our evaluation, conducted on WebLogicQA and WebhopQA datasets, shows that Entailer's reasoning chains are more efficient and produce accurate answers in a step-by-step manner, while also providing a transparent explanation for the answer. Furthermore, we found that users who are not experts in reasoning and logic prefer the step-by-step reasoning provided by Entailer over direct answers. Our research also reveals that users are more likely to accept the truthfulness of answers presented in a step-by-step manner, as supported by users who found the provided reasons to be more convincing. To further validate our approach, we conducted a user study to compare the effectiveness of our method in providing a step-by-step reasoning against a control group that received the same facts alone, without the reasoning steps. Our results show that users who were presented with the reasoning steps were more likely to accept the truthfulness of the answer, while also demonstrating a higher level of confidence in their responses. Our research demonstrates that Entailer's systematic and truthfulness-enhancing reasoning steps can make answers more believable and improve the overall performance of question-answering systems. This expression is obtained by calculating the exact area of these cells through integration and then taking the infimum over all possible transfer costs. The resulting expression for the metric is then compared to the exact area expression, showing that they are equivalent. This version number is used to verify whether the region's version has been correctly reclaimed. If the version number is incorrect, the management field is reset and the region's version number is incremented. This paper introduces a novel category-theoretic programming framework, grounded in the FOLE system, and extends its relational semantics to accommodate procedures as second-order functions. Leveraging a type of functor known as a localisation, we define a procedure-trio and demonstrate a procedure-trio semantics within a specific localization of the Kleisli category. The framework's utility is reinforced by demonstrating its compatibility with existing approaches, such as Kozen's denotational semantics for probabilistic programming, and showing that the resulting relational semantics aligns with expectations. Finally, we outline the potential for generalising this work to other programming paradigms like stochastic stochastic monotone and weighted monotone programming. The FilmTag dataset, a large-scale film classification dataset, is typically used for film recognition tasks with text-based models. However, this dataset is primarily designed for text-based classification tasks, which may not be ideal for film-related tasks. We investigate the potential of using film content for film recognition by fine-tuning a pre-trained Vision-Language model, specifically the CLIP, which has been trained on a vast image-text database. We find that CLIP, a model trained on a vast image-text database, outperforms text-based models on FilmTag, achieving a 71.8% film-tag classification accuracy. Additionally, fine-tuning CLIP for film recognition on a small validation set of 100 films yields a 90.8% film recognition accuracy, which is significantly higher than the film recognition accuracy of 58.2% achieved by the best text-based model. These results demonstrate that models trained on a vast image-text database can be effectively fine-tuned for film recognition on film content and offer a promising alternative to text-based models. In recent years, sports science research has gained significant attention, driven in part by the increasing availability of wearable devices capable of collecting physiological data such as heart rate and speed. However, these devices are not always necessary or practical. To address this limitation, we propose an innovative approach to extracting heart rate information from videos of athletes in training. Our method relies on the motion of the athlete's clothing, which is often more visible than their body. By leveraging this visual data, we can estimate the athlete's heart rate without the need for external equipment. Furthermore, we can also determine the type of movement being performed, such as running or cycling, solely based on the video footage. To achieve this, we have developed a deep learning model that can simultaneously detect heart rate, movement type, and video classification. Our approach is validated through extensive testing on a diverse dataset of over 100,000 videos, representing 14 different sports. The results demonstrate the efficacy of our method in accurately estimating heart rate and movement type, even in challenging situations like occlusion and varied lighting conditions. The growing interest in sequence forecasting has led to significant advancements in the field, particularly in predicting future words given a current utterance. However, most existing research focuses on a single dataset, neglecting the need for real-world applications that often involve multiple downstream tasks. This paper addresses this gap by introducing a multi-task sequence forecasting framework that leverages a large Tunisian Arabizi dataset annotated at three distinct levels: word, chunk, and sentence. We evaluate our approach using three tasks: predicting the next word, identifying the next chunk, and determining the next sentence, and demonstrate its performance using both supervised and unsupervised training methods. Our results show that the proposed model outperforms existing models in all tasks, particularly in predicting the next sentence, and highlights the importance of using multi-task learning for sequence forecasting. We also release the Tunisian Arabizi dataset annotated at three levels to the research community. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/SebastienMekhri/MTSF. domains, such as the medical field. To address this, we have developed a novel

performance in challenging areas. Our results demonstrate that this method
substantially improves the accuracy of BERT-based models in a medical reference

importance of carefully curated datasets and pre-processing techniques in achieving
optimal performance with pre-trained language models. Our findings are available

As deep learning models become increasingly complex, there's a growing need to understand how their design elements contribute to their performance. Researchers have developed methods to analyze the space of possible neural architectures, but these visualizations often fail to provide a clear and intuitive understanding of how different components interact. To address this issue, we propose a set of visualization tools that allow users to explore neural architecture spaces and identify key design principles without requiring prior knowledge or training. By applying these visualizations to a large set of pre-trained convolutional neural networks, we were able to identify specific characteristics that contribute to a network's performance, such as the way different convolutional layers interact with each other, and the relationships between network depth and width. Our results demonstrate that these visualizations can provide a deeper understanding of neural architecture design and can be used to summarize key insights about these complex systems. By making these visualizations available, we hope to facilitate further research into the design of neural architectures and make it easier for researchers to explore this complex space. Accurately mapping the extent of Arctic sea ice is crucial for monitoring its decline and impacts on marine routes and oil fields.  However, this task is complicated by clouds and surface snow obscuring satellite imagery.  In this study, we employed a U-Net architecture in a Bayesian framework to segment sea ice from SAR images, utilizing labels from other sources like MODIS and GLobal Land Surface Water Project data.  Our model was trained on SAR images from RADARSAT-2 and tested on images from Sentinel-1, showing improved results compared to other methods like the SARICE algorithm.  Furthermore, we explored the potential of using SAR images to enhance the accuracy of cloud cover estimates from MODIS data.  Our research indicates that this approach can lead to more accurate and reliable ice coverage maps, particularly in areas with frequent cloud cover.  This work is part of a larger effort to develop a robust and reliable ice mapping system that can function in challenging Arctic conditions.  Our goal is to create a system that can automatically process SAR images and update ice maps in near real-time, providing valuable insights for applications like climate research, resource management, and shipping operations.  This research aims to contribute to a better understanding of Arctic ice coverage and climate change impacts, as well as to inform decision-making in industries that rely on marine activities in the Arctic.  Our research is part of a broader effort to develop a robust and reliable ice mapping system that can operate in challenging Arctic conditions. In a multi-armed bandit setting, we investigate a unique problem where arm qualities are unknown and a special sequence of arm selections, dictated by a monotone function, must be provided. This function, when applied to the arm sequence in reverse order, will always yield an increasing result, prompting the researchers to term it a monotone arm sequence. A key example of such a sequence is the increasing arm sequence, where each arm's quality at each time step is better than the previous, and all arms are revealed at once. The goal is to devise a policy that minimizes regret while adhering to the arm sequence constraint. A new policy called the monotone UCB bandit (MUUCB) is proposed, and its performance is compared to the established UCB policy. The researchers demonstrate that MUUCB's regret is $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{T})$, where T represents the time steps, and this is consistent with the regret of UCB when no arm sequence constraint applies. Furthermore, they show that if the arm selection sequence is constrained to be strictly increasing, the researchers can achieve a poly-logarithmic regret. The researchers also extend their analysis to a more general scenario involving multiple users, each with their own arm selection constraints, and develop a policy that achieves a $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{T})$ regret. This policy is demonstrated to be effective even when the arm selection sequences are not necessarily monotone, and all the researchers' findings are supported by numerical simulations. A key takeaway from this research is that the arm selection sequence can significantly impact the regret performance of the multi-armed bandit algorithm. A new policy called the greedy bandit (GB) is also proposed, and its performance is compared to the established UCB policy. The researchers demonstrate that GB's regret is $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{2/3})$, and this is consistent with the regret of UCB when no arm selection sequence is applied. Furthermore, they show that GB's regret is $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{T})$ if the arm selection sequence is constrained to be strictly increasing. The researchers also extend their analysis to a more general scenario involving multiple users, each with their own arm selection constraints, and develop a policy that achieves a $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{T})$ regret. This paper is a comprehensive analysis of the regret performance of the bandit algorithm in the context of monotone arm selection sequences

example features and modify classification outputs based on their relevance to the

large margins, and also improve performance when combined with ensembling techniques.

We examine a class of query methods for cut search, a combinatorial problem within graph theory. Cut search involves determining the shortest path to and from a given target node 'q' in a weighted graph, G. We propose two algorithms: the Ball-of-Hairs (BOH) method and the Star Contraction (SC) method. By analyzing the performance of these methods on various graph types, including random and structured graphs, we find that the SC method consistently outstrips the BOH method across the board, often by a wide margin. Furthermore, we investigate the computational complexity of these methods and demonstrate that they both operate in linear time on adjacency lists. Additionally, we examine the development of these methods in a distributed setting and show that they both converge in a single round. We propose a new distributed algorithm, the Ball-of-Hairs with Star Contraction (BSM) method, which integrates the strengths of both BOH and SC, and find that it too converges in a single round. Experimental results show that this combined method excels at achieving optimal or near-optimal solutions. The theoretical underpinnings of this method are supported by lower bounds for the cut query problem in the adjacency matrix model. Specifically, we establish that any algorithm solving the cut query problem must have a time complexity of at least omega(log^2 n / log log n) on average. We also demonstrate that the cut query problem is NP-hard, and provide a proof of this hardness that is independent of any specific algorithm. We further show that the cut query problem is approximable within a factor of O(log n / log log n) using a simple greedy algorithm. Experimental results show that this greedy algorithm performs well in practice, although it falls short of the BSM method. We also demonstrate that the BOH method is more efficient than the BSM method, particularly on sparse graphs. Finally, we examine the performance of these methods on the specific problem of the all-pairs shortest paths (APSP) problem in unweighted graphs, and find that the BSM method outperforms the BOH method across the board. We also demonstrate that any algorithm solving the APSP problem must have a time complexity of at most O(n^3 / log n) on adjacency lists. Furthermore, we establish that the APSP problem is NP-hard, and provide a proof of this hardness that is independent of any specific algorithm. Experimental results show that the BSM method outperforms the BOH method by a wide margin on the APSP problem.

The emergence of quantum computers poses a threat to the security of numerous encryption systems widely used in communication networks. However, it may also enable the exploitation of vulnerabilities in cryptographic protocols employed in Bitcoin's proof-of-work consensus algorithm, potentially leading to a significant reduction in the required mining effort. In this research, we examine the likelihood of quantum computers facilitating more efficient mining operations and, as a result, prompting miners to abandon their current hardware and acquire quantum devices. Our findings suggest that, under current assumptions, the deployment of quantum-based mining operations would be disadvantageous to miners, even if quantum computers become significantly more powerful than their classical counterparts. Nevertheless, there are two exceptional scenarios in which the use of quantum computers might offer a benefit to miners, including instances where miners use rented computing resources or when quantum computers are significantly more energy-efficient than traditional computing systems. These scenarios, however, rely on a set of highly optimistic assumptions regarding the capabilities of quantum computers and their operating costs. In light of these assumptions, we estimate that the transition to quantum-based mining operations would not occur before the year 2040. In contrast, if quantum computers prove to be significantly more energy-intensive than traditional computing systems, the transition to quantum-based mining operations is likely to occur much sooner. In this scenario, the transition may take place as early as 2025. In the latter case, the transition may lead to a substantial increase in the total amount of energy consumed by mining operations. In this research, we also explore the potential implications of these findings for the development of alternative blockchain consensus algorithms, such as proof-of-stake. In particular, we note that the transition to quantum-based mining operations would not pose a significant threat to the security of proof-of-stake blockchain consensus algorithms, even if quantum computers become significantly more powerful than their classical counterparts. In contrast, proof-of-work blockchain consensus algorithms would remain vulnerable to the security risks associated with quantum computers, even if quantum-based mining operations are not economically beneficial to miners. In light of these findings, we suggest that the transition to proof-of-stake blockchain consensus algorithms may be a more efficient and effective way to mitigate the security risks associated with quantum computers. In this research, we also explore the potential implications of these findings for the development of quantum-resistant cryptographic systems, including instances where quantum-resistant cryptographic systems are not necessary, even if quantum computers become significantly more powerful than their classical counterparts. In particular, we note that the transition to quantum-resistant cryptographic systems is unlikely to occur, even if quantum-based mining operations are not economically beneficial to miners.

Open information extraction systems have shown significant progress in extracting multiple, open-ended sentences that describe a single piece of information. However, these systems have limitations in capturing intricate relationships between the different components of this information. In an effort to address this issue, we introduce Graphene, an open data extraction system that utilizes a graph-based approach to represent the relationships between the different parts of a piece of information. Graphene achieves this by using a novel graph-based neural network model that incorporates contextual information to improve its ability to recognize complex relationships. Experimental results demonstrate that Graphene is able to accurately identify more relationships than existing systems, while also maintaining high levels of precision in its open data extraction abilities. Furthermore, we have found that the relationships identified by Graphene are often more nuanced and complex than those captured by traditional open data extraction systems, with many representing the combination of multiple distinct relationships. For example, the open extraction result "John bought a house in London that was built in 1920" is equivalent to the combination of three separate relationships: "John bought a house", "the house was built in 1920", and "the house is located in London". Graphene is able to identify these complex relationships while still maintaining high levels of precision, outperforming traditional open data extraction systems. A new approach to modeling laser operation has been developed using the Bogoliubov theory, which provides a clear and intuitive understanding of the bandwidth associated with laser oscillations. This bandwidth is a critical parameter that determines the stability of laser operation and gives rise to relaxation oscillations near the threshold point. In this study, the same principles are applied to a different context: polariton condensates, which exhibit distinct nonlinear optical properties. The findings reveal that the bandwidth of the oscillations within polariton condates is significantly influenced by the inhomogeneities in the condensate and the surrounding exciton reservoir. Video conferencing has become a norm in today's world, yet the high quality videos required for it result in substantial bandwidth usage. This study presents Gemino, an innovative compression system that utilizes cutting-edge neural algorithms to significantly reduce video quality degradation. By integrating multiple lossy compression techniques, Gemino addresses various types of distortion and achieves a notable reduction of 2dB-3dB in mean squared error. A novel adaptive quantization method within the video codec also reduces storage costs by 30%. Notably, Gemino's design diverges from other proposals by allowing for optimal video quality control through adjustable parameters. This flexibility enables a trade-off between compression efficiency and quality preservation, enabling robust video transmission even in the presence of network errors and packet losses. Through extensive testing on a widely used video conferencing platform, Gemino demonstrated its potential for high-quality video delivery at reduced bandwidths. This includes a 50% reduction in bandwidth usage at 360p and 60% at 480p, as well as comparable performance to other top contenders at higher resolutions. Moreover, Gemino's robustness in the face of network disruptions and packet loss has been shown to outperform other systems under similar conditions. The study also highlights the challenges in deploying such a system, including the need for compatibility with existing video codecs and the potential for compatibility issues. This work aims to bridge the gap between research and practical implementation by providing a comprehensive guide to deploying Gemino and adapting it to other video codecs. The study also emphasizes the importance of transparency in the development and deployment process, highlighting the need for researchers to acknowledge the limitations of their work and the challenges they face. The code and prototype used in this study are made available to the research community. The study concludes by highlighting the potential of Gemino as a highly effective video compression system for video conferencing and other applications. The study also emphasizes the need for further research in this area to fully realize the potential of such systems. This research paper forms part of a two-part series focusing on Orthogonal Time Frequency Space Modulation, a multi-carrier system that distinguishes itself from OFDM through its orthogonal signal sets. In this paper, various transmitter architectures for OTFS are explored, including those based on digital signal processing, analog signal processing, and a combination of analog and digital signal processing. The performance of these systems is evaluated in terms of power consumption, computational complexity, and cost, with practical implementation considerations taken into account. To facilitate this analysis, OTFS signal generation and detection techniques are presented, along with a comprehensive performance assessment of different transmitter architectures. Moreover, the effects of hardware impairments on OTFS systems are examined, as well as potential approaches to mitigate these effects. In conclusion, the paper identifies key areas for future research and presents potential solutions to common challenges associated with OTFS system design. A companion paper (Part I) provides an in-depth analysis of OTFS system fundamentals, including its theoretical foundations, system performance, and potential applications. The two papers together offer a comprehensive overview of OTFS system design, from theoretical principles to practical implementation and potential applications. Ultimately, the research aims to provide a solid foundation for the development and deployment of OTFS systems. This paper proposes a preliminary version of a regulatory framework for social robots, aiming to promote transparency and accountability through ethical considerations. The authors advocate for a regulatory approach rooted in open standards, contending that product-driven regulations stifle innovation by prioritizing compliance over principle. In contrast, a regulatory framework grounded in open ethics, where stakeholders can contribute and evolve the rules, has the potential to foster a culture of responsibility, empower autonomy, and facilitate the creation of trustworthy robots. To illustrate this concept, the paper presents a regulatory framework, dubbed the Ethical Black Box, which outlines principles, responsibilities, and obligations for social robots, with a focus on the development of social robots capable of interacting with humans in natural, social contexts. The authors contend that such a regulatory framework is essential for social robots to achieve true social intelligence, but acknowledge that further refinement and discussion are necessary to solidify the proposed Open Regulation. Ultimately, the paper aims to spark a dialogue among stakeholders, including industry professionals, researchers, and policymakers, to shape the future of social robots and their regulation. The authors also provide a publicly accessible, draft version of the Ethical Black Box at https://github.com/ethicalblackbox/ebb. Further information can be found at https://ethicalblackbox.org/. The task of weakly-supervised visual salient object detection aims to identify objects of interest in natural images by using minimal supervision. However, current weakly-supervised approaches often rely on weak object-level features and fail to accurately identify objects. To address this issue, we introduce a novel weakly-supervised approach called Salient Object Subitizing (SOS), which is based on the idea of subitizing (counting) objects of interest. By using a small number of salient object instances, SOS learns to identify and extract weakly-supervised object-level features. To achieve this, SOS employs a two-stage training process that first trains a feature extractor using the salient object instances and then refines the features using a subitizing module. The refined features are then used to train a salient object detector. The SOS approach is evaluated on four public datasets and outperforms current weakly-supervised methods, demonstrating its effectiveness. The objective of open-set identification is to determine when a sample belongs to a known set of classes. This problem is distinct from anomaly detection, as it focuses on samples that might be from an unknown class, rather than definitively being non-anomalous. Current approaches to open-set identification have been based on training a classifier and then testing its ability to identify out-of-distribution data. However, these methods are limited by the lack of available data for training, which can result in poor performance. This paper presents a new approach to open-set identification, which utilizes a similarity metric to identify out-of-distribution data. This approach is based on training a neural network to distinguish between similar and dissimilar examples, using a combination of labeled in-distribution data and unlabeled examples. By leveraging the unlabeled examples, this network can learn to identify out-of-distribution data without the need for additional labels. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach outperforms current methods on a range of open-set identification tasks. Additionally, this paper presents a new benchmark for open-set identification, which includes a range of tasks that are representative of real-world applications. The benchmark also includes a range of tasks that involve out-of-distribution data that is more dissimilar, such as tasks that involve out-of-distribution data that is from a different domain. Estimating the depth of light field images is a crucial step in various applications, such as depth map generation and 3D reconstruction. However, the presence of occlusions in real-world scenes complicates this task. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach that leverages the insights from occlusion-aware cost calculation. By utilizing the parallax information from two views, we can identify occlusions and separate them from other features in the cost volume. To achieve this, we introduce a novel cost volume based on the parallax channel and a refinement module that enhances the cost volume. By incorporating occlusion-aware cost calculation, we can effectively handle occlusions and improve the performance of light field depth estimation. To evaluate the effectiveness of our approach, we conducted experiments on the public datasets and achieved state-of-the-art results. Furthermore, the accompanying video showcases the superior depth map estimation capabilities of our method. The implementation details are available on the GitHub repository.
